idiom_name: private static nested class holding the receiver, arguments and former locals
implementation_notes: Java is the pattern's canonical home. Lambdas, anonymous classes and local classes may only capture final or effectively final locals (JLS chapter 8; Oracle's Local Classes tutorial), so intermediate state that several steps write cannot live in a closure - it must live in fields. Declare a private static nested class in the host, give it a field per argument and former local (plus the host reference only if the algorithm needs it), copy them in through the constructor, move the body into compute(), and leave the host method as a one-line delegation; Extract Method then applies freely inside the class. Keep the class static: an inner class carries a hidden reference to the host instance. Use a local class when the algorithm is used by exactly one method and never inspected, and a lambda only for a single stateless step.
pitfalls: Captured locals must be effectively final, so a lambda cannot replace the field-holding class for any state that is reassigned; wrapping a local in a one-element array or an AtomicInteger to dodge the rule hides the design problem.
If the algorithm calls the host's private methods, extraction forces them to package-private or protected (or duplicates them), coupling the two classes.
Extract a static nested class, not an inner class: the implicit outer reference keeps the host alive as long as the method object is reachable.

variants.name: Record carrier with pure step methods (Java 16+)
variants.idiom_name: record carrying inputs and accumulators, with static pure step methods
variants.implementation_notes: Java 16+ alternative for computations that can be expressed without mutable state: declare a record whose components hold the inputs and every intermediate value, and write the steps as private static methods that take the record and return the next record (or a component). Every step stays independently testable, no field is ever reassigned, and the carrier is immutable; records are implicitly static wherever they are declared, so no outer instance is captured. Choose it when the algorithm is a pipeline of transformations, keep the classic nested class when the steps genuinely share a wide mutable working set, and remember that a record component of reference type is only shallowly immutable.
pitfalls: Records are shallowly immutable: a record component holding a mutable collection or array can still be modified in place by a step.
Threading the state through every signature restores the parameter plumbing the method object removed; when most steps take and return the whole state, the class with fields is the better fit.
